summary: Explains false assumptions people commonly make about DNS names. Because names appear in email addresses, URIs, and other identifiers shown to people, there is strong demand for meaningful names, and application designers often assume more than DNS guarantees. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: People often think internet names work like simple labels. This lists the wrong guesses people make about how those names behave.

questions: what are false assumptions about dns names
why should applications not assume domain name meaning
how do capability negotiation protocols work
subtitle: Why domain names don't reliably predict what services run on them

tldr.problem: People and application designers often assume that a domain name indicates what service or content is available at that address, but DNS makes no such guarantee. A domain like example.cellular could host anything.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies common false assumptions users, clients, and servers make about domain names—such as assuming a www prefix indicates a web server or that a country-code TLD means local content in that language—and explains why these assumptions fail.
tldr.outcome: Applications and servers that ignore domain names and instead use protocol negotiation and capability detection become more robust, interoperable, and resilient to changes.

facts.label: Key principle
facts.value: Never change protocol behavior based on domain name

today: RFC 4367 remains a valid and important guide to application design. It is not a standard but rather a statement of problems that developers have repeatedly encountered. The recommendations reflect decades of Internet protocol design experience.

sections.title: The Problem of Misleading Domain Names
sections.content:
The Domain Name System maps names like example.com to IP addresses. Because these names appear in email addresses, web URLs, and other identifiers that humans read and share, there is strong pressure to register names that sound meaningful—company names, service types, geographic references. A domain like weather.example.com naturally suggests a weather service, and bank.example.com suggests financial services.

The danger is that when these names become embedded in the design of applications and servers, the software begins to assume that a particular service actually runs at that address, even though DNS makes no such guarantee. DNS is purely a mapping service; it cannot enforce what a domain name implies.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet names sound meaningful, so people assume they describe what is really there. But anyone can register any name and put anything behind it. DNS just maps names to addresses—it says nothing about what is there.

sections.title: Three Sources of False Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC models DNS usage as a simple chain: a user enters a domain name, a client application resolves it and contacts a server, and the server responds. Each of these three can make false assumptions.

A user might assume that an email address ending in .gov is from a government employee, or that a URL in an adult-content TLD contains adult material. These assumptions are hard to control but impossible to enforce in software.

A client application might assume that any hostname starting with www is a web server and speak only HTTP, or that a domain name containing the word cellular means the server uses low-bandwidth codecs. If these assumptions are coded into the software, the client fails when they are wrong.

A server might assume that all clients from a particular domain support a specific optional protocol feature, or that clients connecting to a domain labeled for mobile devices have small screens and limited memory. Again, these assumptions cause failures when deployed beyond their presumed audience.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of things make bad guesses from domain names: people reading them, programs sending requests, and programs answering them. Each can be fooled in different ways.

sections.title: How False Assumptions Break Systems
sections.content:
When false assumptions are coded into behavior, several kinds of failures result. An interoperability failure occurs when the client and server disagree on what a protocol requires. If a client assumes a server supports an optional protocol feature and does not implement fallback logic, and the server does not support that feature, the client simply fails. This is a total loss of service that persists until the software is updated.

A system failure can happen when a misinterpretation uncovers a bug. For example, if a server assumes all uploaded files are a particular image format and always sends them to a decompression codec, the codec might crash if it receives a different format.

A poor user experience happens when services work but deliver suboptimal results. A web server that assumes all clients are mobile devices might serve low-resolution images to a user on a desktop computer, or a mail client that assumes a domain name predicts message content might fail to show attachments properly.

Degraded security is perhaps the most concerning: a server might assume all clients support only weak authentication algorithms and ignore requests for stronger ones.
sections.plainLanguage: When code relies on a guessed meaning of a domain name and the guess is wrong, the app breaks, crashes, shows bad results, or even opens security holes.

sections.title: Why Assumptions Become Invalid
sections.content:
Assumptions often make sense at the time they are written, but the Internet environment changes faster than software. Evolution is the primary reason: mobile devices grow more powerful, protocols add new extensions, and standards improve. A server built for the mobile devices of 2000 with small screens and slow processors will fail with modern smartphones. By the time the assumption proves wrong, it is often too late to fix without major engineering effort.

Leakage happens because DNS is global and there is no technical barrier between one domain and another. A server intended for a specific, private community will eventually be found by clients outside that community. The ubiquity of domain names on business cards, web pages, and in shared links makes global discovery inevitable.

Sub-delegation breaks policies. A top-level domain holder might want all servers under .example to follow certain rules, but once subdomains are delegated to other administrators, enforcing consistency becomes nearly impossible. With multiple levels of delegation, ensuring coherent policies across the tree requires extensive human effort and often fails anyway.

Mobility of hosts across networks and providers means a domain name is not a reliable indicator of what access network a host uses. A device might normally run over broadband and carry a domain name from that provider, but later connect via slow wireless while keeping its domain name. The name persists even as the network characteristics change.

Human error in configuration is inevitable. DNS records might not be updated when services move, or a system administrator might apply a policy to one subdomain but forget another.
sections.plainLanguage: Systems change over time, devices get faster, people move things around, and mistakes happen. A guess that was correct once often becomes wrong, and by then it is hard to fix.

sections.title: Design for Robustness Without Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC offers clear recommendations for avoiding these problems. Follow the specifications: when a protocol defines a baseline behavior and optional extensions, implement both. Let the other side negotiate which features it supports; do not assume based on the domain name.

Use capability negotiation: many protocols include mechanisms to discover what the other side supports. HTTP has content negotiation via Accept headers, SIP allows clients to negotiate media types, and MIME systems use Content-Type labels. These mechanisms exist precisely because assumptions fail. Use them.

Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send: this classic Internet principle means preparing for the full range of what a protocol allows another entity to send, rather than limiting what you are willing to receive. Treat domain names as mere addresses, not as hints about service type or capabilities.

The core recommendation is simple: do not change protocol behavior based on the domain name. Use protocol machinery to discover capabilities, follow the specification, and let the endpoints negotiate what they both support.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart systems ask what the other side can do instead of guessing from the name. They follow the rules, use the negotiation tools the protocol provides, and accept whatever the other side sends as long as it is valid.
